text:
An interval tells you which values are plausible. A test asks about one value in particular... usually, could the effect be zero? Say a new checkout converts at eleven point four percent, and the old one at ten point one. But noise makes gaps for free. So the real question is this. If there were no difference at all, how often would chance alone hand you a gap this big?

A test starts from the boring answer: nothing is going on. That's the null hypothesis. The alternative says there's a real effect. Then it asks one thing. If the null were true, would data like mine be surprising? Very surprising, and you reject the null. Ordinary, and you fail to reject it. If that sounds like a trial, it is one.

The null is the defendant, presumed innocent until the evidence says otherwise. Beyond reasonable doubt becomes alpha, the bar the evidence has to clear. Usually five percent, and set before the trial begins. Clear the bar, and the verdict is guilty: reject the null. Fall short, and it's not guilty. And not guilty never means innocent. Failing to reject the null doesn't prove it. The evidence just wasn't strong enough. Here's the whole procedure, once.

An app claims its users walk eight thousand steps a day. Forty of them average seven thousand, four hundred and fifty-three. The null says the true mean is eight thousand. Alpha is five percent, fixed now, before anything is computed. The test statistic measures the gap in units of noise. Here, t is minus two point two four. If the claim were true, a gap at least this big would turn up three percent of the time. That's the p-value. Three is under five, so we reject the claim. Not because we know the true mean, but because eight thousand is hard to believe. And notice: at least this big, in either direction.
